Multi-level spatial model

The spatial model predicts each selection from:

  • distance to the last item (rho_delta),
  • direction relative to the last move (rho_psi),
  • absolute direction (fourier_coef).

The multi-level version, used whenever the data have more than one person, gives each person their own parameter values (u_*) around the condition values, with between-person SDs (sigma_u_*).

We simulate six people with known parameters, fit the model, and check it recovers them.

Code: spatial.R.

# import packages and load our functions
source("../../../../functions/set_up_FoMo.R")
[1] "set_up_FoMo.R: random seed set to 65 (FOMO_SEED)"
# sampler settings (the same in every example; set FOMO_EXAMPLE_ITER for a quick run)
n_iter <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("FOMO_EXAMPLE_ITER", "300"))  # warmup and sampling iterations per chain
n_post_draws <- 50   # posterior draws for posterior predictive simulation

1 Simulate

Six people, \(K = 2\) conditions, 10 trials per person and condition, on a 7 \(\times\) 7 grid with a quarter of cells empty.

spec <- list(
  K = 2,
  nrow = 7, ncol = 7,
  prop_missing = 0.25,
  v_type = "none")

stim <- generate_stim(spec, n_trials = 10, n_people = 6)

The conditions differ in every parameter:

  • Condition one: weaker distance attraction (0.75), turning back (\(-1\)), and moves mostly along the four cardinal directions;
  • Condition two: stronger distance attraction (1.5), carrying on (1), and a strong rightward bias.

Each person’s values vary around these condition values. The simulation draws each between-person SD from an exponential with rate sd_lambda (a larger rate means less spread between people), then each person’s values.

simparams <- list(
  rho_delta_mu = c(0.75, 1.50),
  rho_psi_mu = c(-1, 1),
  # condition one: the four cardinal directions (h4); two: rightwards (h1)
  #                       h1: a, b   h2: a, b   h4: a, b
  fourier_coef_mu = rbind(c(0,   0,     0, 0,     0.8, 0),
                          c(1.5, 0,     0, 0,     0,   0)),
  # random effects: each SD is drawn from exponential(sd_lambda)
  sd_lambda = list(
    rho_delta = c(3, 3),
    rho_psi = c(3, 3),
    fourier_coef = c(4, 4, 4)))

As in the single-level example, we prepare the data and pass it to the simulate version of our Stan model:

sl_sim <- prep_stan_list(stim, simparams)
sim <- sim_fomo(sl_sim, iter = 1, chains = 1)

The simulation selects every item, but real foragers often stop early, so truncate_trials() drops a few selections from the end of each trial: a Poisson(2) number of them, always keeping at least 10. The dropped items stay on the display, unselected. This allows us to test that our model handles inexhaustive data without problems.

extract_pred(sim, stim) |>
  truncate_trials(lambda = 2, min_keep = 10) -> found

found |> group_by(trial) |>
  summarise(n_found = n()) |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable()
trial n_found
1 33
2 37
3 32
4 33
5 35
6 34

By default plot_trial() plots one randomly selected trial per condition.

plot_trial(found, stim)
plot_steps(found)

We can compute a number of trial stats for comparing against the fitted model’s posterior predictions. With several people they are averaged to one row per person and condition, as single trials are noisy.

trial_stats <- compute_trial_stats(found, which_stats = c("spatial", "intersections"))

head(trial_stats) |> knitr::kable()
condition person n_found best_r mean_itd pao n_intersections intersection_rate
one 1 34.2 0.315 0.428 122.83 51.6 1.513
one 2 35.3 0.565 0.209 9.36 3.6 0.101
one 3 34.7 0.628 0.210 11.57 4.7 0.135
one 4 34.8 0.079 0.854 346.93 360.6 10.357

one 6 35.5 0.450 0.285 46.24 14.6 0.412

We also keep each person’s simulated values, to check the per-person estimates against later:

# each person's simulated values
post <- extract_post(sim, found)
groundtruth <- groundtruth_from_sim(simparams, post)

2 Fit

We now fit the multi-level spatial version of FoMo to our simulated data. Four chains of 500 warmup and 500 sampling iterations.

Note: by default the per-person distance effects are centred (centred_params, see prep_stan_list()). With only 10 trials per person that sometimes gives divergent transitions (0 and 22 on two datasets simulated like this one, against none without centring), so here none are centred (centred_params = "none"). The multi-level cat page shows the same check for that model.

sl <- prep_stan_list(stim, found = found,
                     centred_params = "none",
                     save_selections = TRUE)
# a fixed seed, so the chains are the same on every run
fit <- fit_fomo(sl, iter = n_iter, chains = 4, seed = FOMO_SEED)

3 Diagnostics

Posterior medians and 97% HPDIs, the values the data were simulated from (true, and whether each is inside its HPDI), and convergence (R-hat, ESS), for the fixed effects and the between-person SDs (sigma_u_*). Each person’s values (u_*) are summarised in one row per parameter. About one in 33 simulation values should fall outside its HPDI by chance; with six people the SDs are hard to pin down. R-hat above 1.01, or a bulk or tail ESS in the low hundreds, means the chains haven’t mixed well enough to trust the tails of the posterior. The summary’s last line names the worst parameter (random effects included); the table colours R-hat and ESS green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad).

# estimates and convergence, and parameter recovery: are the values used
# to simulate the data inside the posterior's 97% HPDIs?
fomo_summary(fit, sim, random_effects = TRUE, cond_labels = levels(stim$condition))

Recovery: 117 of 128 (91%) simulation values inside the 97% HPDI; about 97% expected by chance.

Convergence (all parameters): largest R-hat 1.012 (sigma_u_fourier_coef[1,3]); smallest bulk ESS 328 (rho_delta[1]), tail ESS 237 (rho_delta[1]); 1 divergent transitions.

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, judged by R-hat and ESS together. Each histogram shows where one chain’s draws rank among all the draws: if the chains have mixed well, every chain’s histogram is roughly flat and they overlap.

plot_post_traces(fit)

log_lik is one value per trial, so loo leaves out a whole trial at a time. A Pareto k above 0.7 marks a trial the fit leans on heavily, whose loo estimate is unreliable. check_high_pareto_k() lists those trials, worst first, with the person each belongs to (z).

loo_result <- fit$loo()
loo_result

4 Posterior

4.1 Posterior densities

Where a posterior sits well inside its prior band, the data rather than the prior set the estimate. A posterior pressed against the edge of its band means the prior is doing some of the work.

post <- extract_post(fit, found, stim)
plot_post(post, groundtruth = groundtruth)

4.2 Each person

Per-person estimates are pulled towards the condition value (shrinkage), most for people whose own data say least. So a person’s interval can miss an extreme simulation value even when the condition values are recovered.

plot_post_per_person_spatial(post, groundtruth)

4.3 Accuracy

  • Deterministic accuracy: how often the item the model judges most likely is the one selected.
  • Probability of the chosen item: the probability the model gave the item that was selected, averaged over selections; it credits the model for being nearly right, not only for top picks.
  • Chance (1 / items left) rises through a trial as fewer items remain.
  • The nearest-neighbour baseline always picks the closest remaining item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity alone.

Note: this is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample accuracy.

plot_post_accuracy(post$acc, stim, found)

5 Posterior predictive check

The model doesn’t predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as many selections as the data have.

sim_post <- sim_fomo(sl, fit, iter = n_post_draws)

extract_pred(sim_post, stim) |>
  semi_join(found, by = c("trial", "n")) -> found_post
plot_trial(found_post, stim)

Finally, we compare the trial statistics between the training data and data simulated from the fitted posterior. As none of the trial statistics are model parameters, reproducing them tests whether the fitted model captures aspects of the behaviour it was not fitted to directly.

sim_stats <- compute_trial_stats(found_post, which_stats = c("spatial", "intersections"))
plot_trial_stats(trial_stats, sim_stats)
